title: LRU Cache: HashMap + doubly linked list, O(1) get/put.
shortTitle: LRU Cache: HashMap plus doubly linked list for O(1) get and put
keyPoints: An LRU cache combines a HashMap (O(1) key lookup) with a doubly linked list (O(1) reorder and eviction)
The doubly linked list orders entries by recency: most recently used at the head, least recently used at the tail
Sentinel head and tail nodes eliminate null checks on insertion and removal at the ends
On get: look up in map, move node to head; on put: insert at head, evict from tail if over capacity
When evicting, you must remove the key from the map as well as the node from the list to prevent memory leaks
Java's LinkedHashMap with access order is a shortcut, but building it by hand demonstrates the mechanics interviewers want

s1_definition.oneliner: A hash map finds the node instantly and a doubly linked list reorders it instantly, so every get and put runs in constant time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **LRU Cache** – a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently used entry when full.
- **HashMap** – maps each key to its doubly linked list node for O(1) lookup.
- **Doubly linked list** – maintains usage order; most recently used at one end, least recently used at the other.
- **Sentinel nodes** – dummy head and tail eliminate edge-case null checks for insertions and removals.
- **Eviction** – when capacity is exceeded, remove the node just before the tail (least recently used) and delete its key from the map.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India teller keeps only the twenty most recently touched customer files on the desk. Every time a file is read or updated, it moves to the front of the pile. When a brand new file arrives and the desk is full, the file at the very back, the one nobody has touched in the longest time, is put back in the archive. The desk is the cache, the pile order is the linked list, and the quick index of where each file sits is the hash map.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  LRU Cache Structure

  HashMap: { ACC-001 → node1, ACC-003 → node3, ACC-004 → node4 }

  Doubly Linked List (most recent → least recent):
  [HEAD] <──> [ACC-004] <──> [ACC-001] <──> [ACC-003] <──> [TAIL]
  sentinel                                               sentinel

  get(ACC-001): move ACC-001 to head
  [HEAD] <──> [ACC-001] <──> [ACC-004] <──> [ACC-003] <──> [TAIL]

  put(ACC-005): insert at head, evict ACC-003 (before tail)
  [HEAD] <──> [ACC-005] <──> [ACC-001] <──> [ACC-004] <──> [TAIL]
  map.remove("ACC-003")
```

```text
  Node Operations

  Remove node X:
    X.prev.next = X.next
    X.next.prev = X.prev

  Add after head:
    X.prev = HEAD
    X.next = HEAD.next
    HEAD.next.prev = X
    HEAD.next = X
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An LRU cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently used entry when full. The O(1) design combines a hash map for instant key lookup with a doubly linked list for instant reordering. The list keeps entries ordered by recency: the most recently used node sits right after a sentinel head, and the least recently used sits right before a sentinel tail.

On `get`, the map finds the node and the list moves it to the head. On `put`, a new node is inserted at the head and added to the map; if that pushes the size over capacity, the node just before the tail is evicted from both the list and the map. Removing the evicted key from the map is critical: forgetting it causes memory leaks and stale lookups.

Sentinel head and tail nodes are what make the doubly linked list operations clean. They ensure every real node always has valid `prev` and `next` neighbors, eliminating null checks for empty-list and single-element edge cases.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, the account service caches hot account balances in an LRU cache. A frequently checked account is promoted on every access and never evicted by a burst of unrelated lookups, keeping the cache hit rate high and the database load low. For production use, we wrap the cache with synchronization for thread safety.

Remember one sentence: a hash map gives O(1) lookup and a doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering, together they make get and put constant time in an LRU cache.
